291.main_claim: Resolutions fail because January 1 supplies a borrowed reason to start, so once the date passes nothing in ordinary life keeps prompting them and they are simply forgotten.
choices: blames the calendar date rather than willpower
author admits forgetting rather than failing resolutions
start when the reason appears and write down why
hook habits to weekly routines and book a mid-February check-in
291.quality_reason: Fresh, coherent argument in a warm personal voice with practical tips; on length and ready to post.

317.main_claim: Resolutions fail not from laziness but because they are vague wishes, too big, willpower-dependent and broken by a single slip.
choices: four bolded causes then five bulleted fixes
317.quality_reason: Solid, accurate standard listicle, but leaves '[unchecked]' markers in the text that must be removed before posting.

362.main_claim: Most people don't quit their resolutions; they forget them, because they're made on a whim at a midnight party with no reminder or plan.
choices: New Year's Eve party scene opening
write it down in daylight and pick one
lock-screen reminder, calendar check-ins, a friend who asks
playful aside recruiting readers as accountability friends
362.quality_reason: Vivid, cohesive and personal with a clear twist and actionable tips; fits a personal blog perfectly.

414.main_claim: Resolutions fail because of how they are built, as vague wishes stacked all at once with streak thinking and outcome focus, not because people lack willpower.
choices: pick one small thing, attach it to a routine, be patient
414.quality_reason: Clear, accurate and friendly with a light personal touch; familiar content but polished and ready to use.

429.main_claim: Losing motivation is inevitable, so resolutions fail when nothing but motivation holds them up; having someone who asks is what keeps them going.
choices: author's 700-day Welsh streak with their 12-year-old daughter
hang the asking on an existing routine; keep it small enough to answer yes
offer to be readers' accountability person
429.quality_reason: Distinctive personal anecdote drives a clear, coherent argument with practical takeaways; reads as genuinely the author's own.

480.main_claim: Resolutions fail because January is the wrong season to start anything, so like gardeners we should plan in winter and start in spring.
choices: extended gardening metaphor (sowing beans in January)
winter is for planning, not planting
start the resolution in spring when the first seeds go in
480.quality_reason: Charming, coherent metaphor sustained well for a gardening blog; a bit repetitive in the middle.

548.main_claim: Resolutions fail because motivation always runs out and most have nothing, such as a person checking in, to carry them once it does.
choices: do it with someone and tie check-ins to daily events
548.quality_reason: Good argument and voice, but leaves bracketed placeholders for the author to fill in, so it can't be posted as is.

575.main_claim: Many resolutions fail because of timing, since January is a season of rest, and like gardeners we should plan in winter and begin in spring.
choices: use winter to plan and reflect on obstacles
start as days lengthen in spring
575.quality_reason: Warm, coherent and well paced for a gardening-minded reader; slightly softer and less pointed than it could be.

587.main_claim: Resolutions fail not from lack of willpower but because they are vague, overloaded, tied to an arbitrary date, derailed by all-or-nothing thinking and focused on outcomes over systems.
choices: five bolded causes plus bulleted fixes
587.quality_reason: Well-organized, accurate, crisply written standard take with useful advice; ready to post.

620.main_claim: Resolutions fail mainly because they are vague, and making them specific and small makes them stick.
620.quality_reason: Punchy, funny and accurate with properly hedged stats; conventional advice but polished.

657.main_claim: Most resolutions fail for structural reasons such as vagueness, overreach, clashing routines, all-or-nothing thinking and arbitrary timing rather than weak willpower.
choices: fighting old cues and defaults (takeout example)
pick one small thing and plan for misses
657.quality_reason: Clear, sensible and well written with good concrete examples; standard but fully usable.

713.main_claim: Resolutions fail from bad timing, not weak willpower, so treat them like a planting plan: decide in winter and start in spring.
choices: winter is for planning at the kitchen table
give the resolution a post-frost start date
713.quality_reason: Vivid, tight and consistently argued metaphor with a concrete takeaway; polished and blog-ready.

747.main_claim: Resolutions fail because of how we set them up, with outcome goals, too much too fast, all-or-nothing thinking, arbitrary timing and no real 'why'.
choices: smaller promises attached to existing routines
747.quality_reason: Clean, accurate and readable standard take with sensible advice; ready to use.

811.main_claim: Resolutions fail because they ask us to beat our lazy default every day, so we should design our surroundings to make laziness work for us.
choices: do the hard setup once, e.g. automatic savings
add friction to bad habits and shrink the daily ask
811.quality_reason: Bold, coherent thesis with practical environment-design tips; the blunt framing may not suit every personal blog.

910.main_claim: Resolutions fail because motivation inevitably fades and most have nothing else to run on; tying one to a person or routine keeps it alive.
choices: tie the resolution to a person or routine
910.quality_reason: Warm, personal and coherent with a nice sign-off; advice is lighter and the motivation point is a bit repetitive.

928.main_claim: January is a terrible time to start anything, and resolutions tied to the calendar rather than a personal reason fade with the novelty.

pick your own personal start date
928.quality_reason: Funny, well-sourced and balanced (concedes the fresh-start effect), with clear tips; excellent personal-blog piece.
